blocks.title: Nutrition for Hypertrophy on a Tight Budget

blocks.content: Target the same 1.6-2g/kg protein daily as any hypertrophy diet, built entirely around India's cheapest protein staples: eggs (roughly ₹6-7 each, 6g protein), soya chunks (roughly ₹150-200/kg dry, ~52g protein per 100g), moong or chana dal (roughly ₹100-140/kg, ~20-24g protein per 100g dry), and milk (roughly ₹55-65/litre, 3.2g protein per 100ml). Buying dal, rice, and soya chunks in 5-10kg sacks from a local kirana or wholesale market cuts per-kg cost noticeably compared to small daily purchases, and batch-cooking dal or boiling a dozen eggs at once saves both money and prep time across the week.

Recovery costs nothing extra — sleep, consistent training, and stress management matter exactly as much here as in any budget bracket. The most common mistake on a tight budget is skipping meals to save money rather than choosing cheaper, protein-dense staples over expensive convenience or packaged foods — a missed meal costs more in lost muscle-building progress than the small amount of money it saves.

blocks.title: Don't Sacrifice Protein to Save on Groceries
blocks.content: If money is genuinely tight, cut back on expensive extras (juices, packaged snacks, eating out) before cutting protein sources — eggs, dal, and soya chunks remain some of the cheapest calories and protein available regardless of budget constraints.

Myth: you need whey protein to build muscle. Fact: whey is convenient but not necessary — a well-planned whole-food diet using eggs, dal, soya, and milk can fully match its protein delivery at a lower or comparable cost per gram once bulk buying is factored in. Myth: mass gainers are an efficient way to hit calorie targets on a budget. Fact: mass gainers are often expensive per calorie compared to home-made options like a banana-milk-peanut shake or extra rice and ghee, which deliver similar calories far more cheaply. If any supplement fits a tight budget, creatine monohydrate is the best value — it's inexpensive per dose (roughly ₹8-12/day) and has strong evidence behind it; skip pricier extras. Deload every 6-8 weeks — this costs nothing and protects the training investment you've already made.

blocks.title: The Milk-Banana-Peanut Budget Shake
blocks.content: Blend 300ml milk, 1 banana, and a tablespoon of peanut butter for a homemade post-workout shake with roughly 15-18g protein and 400+ calories at a fraction of the cost of a commercial mass gainer.

A tight food budget is a planning problem, not a hypertrophy problem. Eggs, soya chunks, dal, and milk deliver muscle-building protein at some of the lowest costs per gram available anywhere, and bulk buying plus batch cooking stretches every rupee further. Combine this with a standard progressive-overload training split and you have every ingredient needed for real muscle growth — no imported supplements required.

faq_schema.question: Can I build muscle without buying whey protein or other supplements?
faq_schema.answer: Yes. Whole-food sources like eggs, soya chunks, dal, and milk can fully cover daily protein needs for muscle building. Whey is a convenience product, not a requirement — a well-planned whole-food diet works just as well.

faq_schema.question: What are the cheapest high-protein foods available in India?
faq_schema.answer: Eggs, soya chunks, moong/chana dal, and milk are consistently among the cheapest sources of protein per gram in India, especially when dal, rice, and soya chunks are bought in bulk from a kirana or wholesale market.

faq_schema.question: How much money do I need to spend daily on food to build muscle?
faq_schema.answer: A realistic budget of roughly ₹150-200/day can support 120-140g of protein and adequate calories for muscle building when built around eggs, dal, soya chunks, milk, and seasonal vegetables rather than packaged or premium foods.

faq_schema.question: Is it worth buying a mass gainer to hit calorie targets cheaply?
faq_schema.answer: Usually not — mass gainers tend to be expensive per calorie compared to home-made options like a milk, banana, and peanut butter shake or an extra portion of rice and ghee, which deliver similar calories at a much lower cost.

faq_schema.question: Which single supplement is worth buying on a tight budget?
faq_schema.answer: Creatine monohydrate offers the strongest evidence-to-cost ratio, typically costing around ₹8-12 per daily dose, and is a better use of a limited supplement budget than pricier options like BCAAs or fat burners.
